body_markdown:
As all car nerds know, details matter. A tiny badge that 90% of people won’t notice or care about can be the difference between a “meh” and a “whoahhh.” What that badge means, and all the goodies it comes with, can also make a big difference in a car’s value. Sometimes it’s a huge difference. Trims, colors, engines, transmissions, or other options all contribute, just like a car’s condition.


We had this dynamic in mind recently when poring over some data for the Hagerty Price Guide, and discovered which submodels within a vehicle generation make the biggest difference in condition #2 (excellent) value compared to the base model. Think standard[C5 Corvette](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/2003/2003-chevrolet-corvette-base?id=aCn1I000000DMQuSAO) vs. a[Z06](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/2003/2003-chevrolet-corvette-z06?id=aCn1I000000CrvHSAS) , just on a grander scale. Below are some of the biggest deltas we found.


## [Mercedes-Benz SLS Black Series](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=mercedes-benz+sls)


**SLS AMG Coupe:** $323,000


Broad Arrow


**SLS AMG Black Series:** $549,000


Daimler AG


The first Mercedes designed from scratch by AMG, the SLS ( *Super Leicht Sport* , or “Super Light Sport”) packs a 6.2-liter, naturally aspirated V-8 putting down 563 hp and 479 lb-ft through an AMG Speedshift seven-speed dual-clutch automatic transaxle. On top sits an aluminum body, opened via a pair of gullwing doors. *Motor Trend* called it a “commuter/carver: like a fighter/bomber, it’s good at both, excellent at neither.” When new, the coupe version cost about $200K.


The ultimate version of the 2010–15 SLS is the Black Series, introduced in 2013. Inspired by the GT3 race version of the SLS, it came with 622 hp, 468 lb-ft, and a booming 8000 rpm redline. Extensive use of carbon fiber, a titanium exhaust, a lower-mounted gearbox with faster shifts and a shorter axle ratio, new suspension, wider track, and better brakes rounded out the package. Just 132 made it to the U.S., and they cost about 75 grand more than the standard car, which seems like good value considering the extent of the upgrades.


Not such a good value today, though. Both versions have surged in value this year, and both are currently worth more than their inflation-adjusted MSRP, but the Black Series rose at a sharper clip, as demand for high-tier Benzes is very high.


## [Ferrari F430 Scuderia](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=ferrari+f430)


**F430 Coupe:** $191,000


Broad Arrow


**F430 Scuderia:** $707,000


Broad Arrow


In 2004, Ferrari was on a hot streak. On track, the Scuderia was on its way to a fifth straight Formula 1 World Championships, and the[Enzo](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/enzo/2003/2003-ferrari-enzo-base?id=aCn1I000000DI6oSAG) was the high-performance benchmark for road cars. The new F430 also significantly raised the bar for V-8 supercars, boasting tech adapted from F1, numerous styling cues from the flagship Enzo, and a long list of improvements over the[360 Modena](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/360/2002/2002-ferrari-360-modena?id=aCn1I000000DI2MSAW) that preceded it.


In 2007, Ferrari won the F1 World Championship again and introduced the F430 Scuderia to celebrate. This more track-oriented version shed 220 pounds, gained 13 horsepower (to 503 total), and could hit 202 mph thanks to revised aerodynamics. When new, a standard F430 coupe would have cost about 180 grand, while the Scuderia upped the ante by about 100 grand.


Today, the difference is much more pronounced, to say the least. Scuderias have been one of the biggest winners in 2026’s frenzy for rare-spec modern Ferraris, and their values have more than doubled compared to this time in 2025. Base models have grown significantly, too, just at a more relatively modest 29%. The difference is even more pronounced with open cars. An F430 Spider in #2 condition is currently worth $207K on average, while the Scuderia 16M (the Spider version of the Scuderia) is worth over $1M.


## [Dodge Charger Daytona (Hemi)](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1969+dodge+charger+hemi)


**Charger Hardtop Coupe** : $177,000


Mecum


**Charger Daytona:** $729,000


Mecum


The updated ’68 Charger was only available in one body style, but there were multiple trims from which a prospective Mopar muscle car buyer could choose, along with several hefty V-8s. The 426-cid/425-hp Hemi, of course, was at the top of the lineup. And in 1969, Chrysler massaged the Charger into its first “aero” car aimed at the high-speed ovals of NASCAR racing. The pointy-nosed, high-winged Daytona won its first race and notched six total NASCAR victories during the 1969 and ’70 seasons. In order to homologate it for the track, Dodge sold 503 Charger Daytonas to the public, with 70 of them powered by Hemis.


The $177K figure on the left photo is the average #2 condition value for all Hemi-powered “regular” 1968–70 Chargers. A “regular” Hemi Charger, then, is hardly a cheap car, but adding on the high-speed appendages of the Daytona more than quadruples the price. Chrysler’s follow-up to the Daytona, the nearly identical but more common Plymouth Road Runner Superbird, doesn’t command quite as big of a premium. The average #2 value for a regular Hemi-powered[Road Runner](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/plymouth/road_runner/1970/1970-plymouth-road_runner-base?id=aCn1I000000CruDSAS) is $132,500, compared to $384,000 for the[Hemi Superbird](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/plymouth/road_runner/1970/1970-plymouth-road_runner-superbird?id=aCn1I000000DSN8SAO) .


## [Aston Martin DB4 GT Zagato](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=aston+martin+db4)


**DB4 Coupe:** $520,000


Matthew Howell


**DB4 GT Zagato:** $9,950,000


Rex Gray


Built from 1958 through 1963 and styled by Carrozzeria Touring in Milan, the DB4 was an elegant departure from the[DB2](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=aston+martin+db2) road cars that came before it, and it helped establish a signature look for Aston Martin going forward.


DB4 production totaled over 1200 cars, with running changes in exterior and mechanical details along the way. There were also competition variants, starting with the DB4 GT, of which 95 were built. With twin ignition, triple Weber carbs, and higher compression, Aston wrung another 60 hp out of the 3.7-liter straight-six, while thinner bodywork with faired-in headlights and a shorter wheelbase shaved nearly 200 pounds of mass.


The DB4 GT is already a top-shelf classic with a condition #2 value of $2.8M, but from a collector standpoint, the ultimate DB4s are the 19 cars bodied by another Milanese coachbuilder, Zagato. Even lighter and more striking to look at than the DB4 GT, the DB4 GT Zagato didn’t find massive success on track; it’s still one of the most valuable cars to wear the Aston Martin wings, and exists on a completely different value plane than a standard DB4. A couple of them have sold for eight figures at auction, and the current #2 value is just under $10M.


## [Porsche 356A Carrera Speedster](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=porsche+356a+speedster)


**356A Speedster:** $400,000


Broad Arrow


**356A Carrera:** $1,322,000


Mecum


Porsche likes to reuse names about as much as George Foreman, and “Carrera” has meant all sorts of different things over the years. It first adorned a P-car in the ’50s, though, as a nod to the company’s success in Mexico’s grueling Carrera Panamericana road race.


To a 356 buyer, “Carrera” referred to the company’s sophisticated 1.5-liter four-cam flat-four, aka the Type 547, aka the Fuhrmann engine. Available as an option starting with the 356A in 1955, it was far more powerful than the visually almost identical pushrod-powered cars but also far more expensive, so it was never a big seller even though Porsche offered it all the way up to the end of 356 production in 1965.


Carrera-powered cars are also far more expensive today, and the difference is most pronounced in 356A Speedsters (1955–59). Four cams, triple the price.
